Heterologous protein expression in insect cells.
We used the flashBACTM system (Oxford Expression Technologies) for recombinant protein expression using a baculovirus system 27, 28, 29 following the manufacturer recommendations. Briefly, Sf9 insect cells (Oxford Expression Technologies) were seeded in a 6 wells/plate at a density of 0.3-0.5 x 106 cells/mL in serum free Sf900-II media (Gibco) supplemented with 200 μL of Gentamycin (50 mg/mL) per liter. Next, the transfection reaction was prepared in a sterile Eppendorf tube containing antibiotic-free media Sf900-II (up-to 1 mL) and the transfection mixture composed by: 2.5 μL of flashBacTM linear viral DNA (20 ng/ L), 1 L (500 ng) of transfer plasmid (pBacPAK3) and 5 μL of transfection reagent (Fugene) following manufacturer instructions. After 5-6 days, the supernatant of the transfected cells was collected to have the recombinant baculovirus stock (P1). The P1 baculovirus was inoculated (1:25) in a suspension culture of 25 mL of complete Sf900-II media at a density of 1.5-2 x 106 cells/ml and incubated shaking at 90-95 rpm for 3-4 days. After this time, the supernatant was recovered obtaining the P2 baculovirus stock. After testing the expression of the protein, the P2 baculovirus was used to inoculate another 100 mL suspension culture of Sf9 cells as indicated before at a 1:100 dilution. After 3-4 days (72-96 hours), the supernatant became the P3 baculovirus stock. Both, the P2 and P3 baculovirus were used as baculovirus stocks for protein production.

Protein purification.
Protein purification was achieved by in tandem immobilized metal ion affinity (Ni+2) and Glutathione-conjugated gravity flow chromatography and in-gel 3C-protease digestion followed by size exclusion chromatography if required. This optimized protocol resulted in a highly pure and monodisperse recombinant fusion product. Inoculated insect cell cultures (72-96 hours) were harvested by centrifugation at 1800 g (Eppendorf Centrifuge 5810 R) during 10 min at 4ºC. Pellets were stored at -80 ºC or used directly for protein purification. Pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 10 mM Benzamidine, 0.2 mM AEBSF, 2 mM TCEP). After sonication on ice (20 cycles 9 seconds on/ 3 seconds off and 37% amplitude), crude lysates were centrifugated at 33000g/48000 g (JA 25-50 rotor, Beckman Coulter Avanti J-25) at 4 ºC for 45 min. Clarified lysate underwent a final sonication step of 10 sec followed by filtration with a 45 m filter (Jet Biofilter) with a syringe. Crude lysate, clarified lysate (supernatant) and insoluble material (pellet) samples were mixed with 5X Laemmli sample buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and run on SDS-Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). First, the clarified lysate was incubated with a previously equilibrated Nickel (Ni2+) chelate resin. After two hours incubation on rotation in a cold room, the flow through (FT) was separated and beads were washed with Buffer A (20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP) with additional 20 mM Imidazole. Protein elution was done with Buffer B (20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 400 mM Imidazole, 2 mM TCEP) using a filter spin column (SC 1000-1KT, Lot SLCD4489, SIGMA-ALDRICH) by centrifugation at 6000g (Eppendorf centrifuge 5415D) during 2 min. Fractions were checked by SDS-PAGE stained with Coomassie previously to the second purification step. Positive fractions eluted from the His-affinity step were incubated with Glutathione conjugated Sepharose beads (Glutathione Sepharose® 4 Fast Flow, Cytiva) for several hours at 4 ºC. Next, the GST-tagged protein was separated by centrifugation at 160g (Eppendorf Centrifuge 5810 R) and washed 4-5 times with 10 mL of GST-Buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT) prior to in gel digestion (3-4 hours) with an GST-3C protease (200 g/L culture) and elution (2-3) using a filter spin column at 6000g for 2 min (Eppendorf centrifuge 5415D). Eluted fractions were checked by SDS-PAGE gel stained with Coomassie. Protein concentration and purity were measured by absorbance using a Nanodrop. When required, a size exclusion chromatography (SEC) step using AKTA pure protein purification system (GE Healthcare) was performed. The sample was concentrated up to 2 mL with a Millipore concentrator with a 30 kDa cut-off by centrifugation at 800g (Eppendorf Centrifuge 5810 R) at 4 ºC. The concentrated sample was injected into a Superdex 200 16/60, 10/300 or 3.2/300 columns (GE Healthcare). The input of the column together with the collected fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE followed by Coomassie staining, and the protein concentration was measured by absorbance.

SDS-PAGE, western blotting and antibodies.
Proteins were electrophoretically separated on 12% SDS-PAGE gels run in the Mini-PROTEAN system with electrophoresis buffer (25 mM Tris pH 8.3, 192 mM glycine, 0.1% SDS) by using a BIO RAD PowerPac Basic at a constant voltage of 150-200 mV for 30-45min. Pre-stained dual colour markers (Precision Plus Protein Standards 10-250 kDa, BIO-RAD and Protein Ladder PS10 Plus 11-180 kDa, GeneOn) were used as molecular weight standards. For protein staining, gels were gently shacked in Coomassie staining solution (10% acetic acid, 40% absolute ethanol and 50% MilliQ water with 1g/L Brilliant blue 250 R) for 30-60 min. Then the gels were distained for 1-2 hours with a distaining solution (10% acetic acid, 50% absolute ethanol, 40% MilliQ water). Proteins were transferred from SDS-PAGE gels onto nitrocellulose 0.2 m (Amersham) or PVDF 0.45 m (Millipore) membranes using the Mini-PROTEAN system (BIO RAD). Before transference, PVDF membranes were activated first in ethanol 100% for 10 min. Membrane were wet-transferred in transfer buffer (25 mM Tris pH 8.8, Glycine 190 mM and ethanol 10%) on ice at constant 100-200 V for 60 min. Next, transferred membranes were blocked in TBS (10 mM Tris pH 8, 150 mM NaCl) supplemented with 5% (w/v) skimmed powder milk and gently shacked for 30 min. After blocking step, membranes were washed in TBS-T (10 mM Tris pH 8, 150 mM NaCl Tween-20 0.1% v/v) for 3-4 times. Then they were incubated with constant agitation (Duomax 1030, Heidolph) O/N at 4ºC with the following primary antibodies diluted in TBS-T supplemented with 5% BSA (w/v): phospho-Tyr (pTyr-100, CST #9411), RET (D3D8R, CST #14698), phospho-Ret Tyr 905 (CST #3221), phospho-Ret Tyr 1015 (Abcam # 74154) and phospho-Ret Tyr 1062 (Abcam # 51103) at 1:5.000 or 1:10.000 dilution. After overnight incubation with the primary antibody, membranes were washed with TBS-T for 3-4 times and incubated with the secondary antibody for 60 min with gently shaking protected from light. Secondary antibodies used were anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) conjugated at 800 nm (DyLight 800 Conjugate #5151, CST) and anti-mouse IgG (H+L) conjugated at 680 nm (DyLight 680 Conjugate #5470, CST). These secondary antibodies were diluted 1:20.000 in TBS-T with 5% (w/v) skimmed powder milk. After 60 min of secondary antibody incubation, membranes were washed with 20mL of TBS-T for 3-4 times. Finally, proteins were detected in the membranes with the Odyssey CLx scanner (LI-COR Biosciences) and the images were analyzed with the Image Studio lite software.

Differential Scanning Fluorimetry.
To determine the thermal stability of the recombinants proteins we apply a direct method of Differential Scanning Fluorimetry (DSF) based on intrinsic fluorescence (IF) detection using a Tycho NT.6 instrument (NanoTemper Technologies). Briefly, a protein sample (1-2 M, 12L) was loaded into a glass capillary tube and heated from 35 ºC to 95 ºC at a rate of 30 ºC /min. The inflection temperatures (T) were calculated by the instrument based on the 350/330nm fluorescence ratio. We measure the increment in thermal stability in the absence or presence of different ligands and inhibitors, as indicated in the text.

Mass Photometry.
To determine the molecular mass distributions (40 kDa to 5 MDa) of single molecules we applied light scattering to detect individual, unlabeled molecules in dilute solutions using a MPone instrument (Refeyn). All the events were recorded with Refeyn Acquire MP software and analyzed with Refeyn Discover MP software to obtain mass distribution of protein samples.

In vitro phosphorylation assays.
For autophosphorylation experiments, recombinant protein 1-2 M (final concentration) was used in 20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 2mM DTT and 2 mM MgCl . We performed a time-points reaction triggered by the addition of ATP (1 mM): unstimulated, 1, 5, 15, 30 min. To stop the phosphorylation reaction samples were mixed with 5X Laemmli sample buffer and denaturalized at 95ºC during 2-5 min in a thermoblock (AccuBlock, Labnet). In the case of phosphorylation experiments using intact substrate surrogates (catalytic dead) a 1:3 molar excess of the substrate to the enzyme was employed in the reaction. For the nucleotide titration experiments the phospho-tyrosine activity of CCDC6-RET was monitored under increasing concentrations of nucleotide (from 10 to 5000 M) after 1-15 min stimulation.
For the time course autophosphorylation assays using radiolabeled nucleotides we prepared an in vitro time course autophosphorylation reaction as follow: for ATP (P32, Revvity) we performed a 0-30 min time course assay in elution buffer 20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT and 4 mM MgCl complemented with kinase (2.5 M), ATP (2 mM) and ATP P32 (50 Ci). In the case of the radioactive assay with ADP (P33, Hartmann Analytics), for the time course of the autophosphorylation reaction (0-60 min) buffer was complemented with kinase (10 M), ADP (1 mM) and ADP P33 (60 Ci). Samples were mixed with 5X Laemmli sample buffer and denaturalized at 95ºC during 2-5 min before being run on a 4-12% precast bis-tris polyacrylamide gels (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Electrophoresis was run at 200 V, after which the gels were introduced in a exposure cassette with a phosphor screen for 2-4 hours first, and then overnight for a longer exposure if required. Screens were developed in an Amersham Typhoon Biomolecular scanner using the phosphor imaging option using 4000 volts and 100 µM of pixel size resolution.

Enzyme kinetic assays.
Rates of phospho-tyrosine activity by recombinant CCDC6-RET and its variants were determined by a continuous ATP-coupled pyruvate kinase essay based on the consumption of NADH in the absence and presence of different peptides substrates at increasing concentrations of ATP 28, 29, 30. The enzyme-substrate solution (1 mM Tris-Cl pH 7.5, 1 mM MgSO , 400 mM phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), 100 mM NADH, 2450 U/mL Pyruvate kinase, 2.26 mg/mL Lactate dehydrogenase) was prepared at different concentrations of ATP (mM): 0, 0.08, 0.16, 0.32, 0.65, 1.25, 2.5 and 5. Unless otherwise stated, the final protein concentration used in these assays was 0.2-1 M, and the concentration of the peptides used EAIYAAPFAKKK and the RET A-loop DVYEEDSYV were 1.35 and 0.55 mM, respectively. The experiments were performed in a 384 well plate (Greiner bio-one) and the NADH consumption was read at 340 nm wavelength during 120 cycles of 30 sec each by using a microplate reader (CLARIOstar Plus, BMG LABTECH). NADH consumption curves were obtained, and slopes were calculated by using de CLARIOstar Data Analysis software. Finally, by using Prism software, catalytic rates and kinetic constants were obtained by fitting the data to the Michaelis-Menten equation.

Mass Spectrometry.
For liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) samples (2.5-5 M) were reduced and alkylated in 15 mM TCEP and 30 mM CAA for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. Proteins were then digested overnight at 37 °C with trypsin (Promega) in 1 M urea, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, using an estimated protein-to-enzyme ratio of 100:1. Digestion was quenched with 0.1% TFA and resulting peptides were desalted using C18 stage-tips. LC-MS/MS analysis was performed on a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system. Digested peptides were loaded into a trap column (Acclaim™ PepMap™ 100 C18 LC Columns 5 µm, 20 mm length) for 3 min at a flow rate of 10 µL/min in 0.1% formic acid, and then separated on an EASY-Spray PepMap RSLC C18 column (2 µm, 75 µm x 50 cm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 45 °C using a 60 min effective gradient (buffer A: 0.1% FA; buffer B: 100% ACN, 0.1% FA) at a flow rate of 250 nL/min. The gradient used was, from 4% to 6% B in 2 min, from 6% to 33% B in 58 min, plus 10 additional min at 98% B.
Peptides were ionized using an EASY-Spray source at 1.5 kV with a capillary temperature of 300 °C. The mass spectrometer was operated in a data-dependent acquisition mode (DDA using a top 15 method with an intensity threshold of ≥ 4.5 x 104, a dynamic exclusion of 5 or 10 sec and excluding unassigned, +1 and > +6 charged ions. Full MS scans (350–1500 m/z) were acquired at 70,000 resolution (FWHM at 200 m/z), followed by MS/MS scans at 35,000 resolution using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD, NCE 27). The isolation window was 2.0 Th. Ion targets were 3×10⁶ for MS (max IT 25 ms) and 1×10⁵ for MS/MS (max IT 110 ms).
Raw files were processed with Maxquant (v 1.6 and higher) using the default settings against a database containing the sequences of the recombinant proteins. Carbamidomethylation of cysteines was set as a fixed modification whereas oxidation of methionines, acetylation and phosphorylation of serines, threonines and tyrosines were set as variable modifications. Minimal peptide length of seven amino acids and a maximum of two tryptic missed cleavages were allowed. Results were filtered at 1% FDR at both peptide and protein levels. Raw data were imported into Skyline. Quantitative analysis was performed in Skyline. Label free quantification of phosphopeptides was performed by integrating the extracted ion chromatogram (XIC) of the isotopic envelope. Only interference-free peaks were used for quantification. Phosphopeptides intensities were normalized by the intensity of the non-modified peptides of the target protein.
Data shown are from four independent autophosphorylation experiments with two technical replicates each (see supplementary tables 1-4). Phospho sites that are consistent across the different datasets are summarized on main table 1.

Crosslinking mass spectrometry.
Both phosphorylated (1 mM ATP, 2 mM MgCl , 30 min) and un-phosphorylated CCDC6-RET (6 µM) were crosslinked with 200-fold molar excess of disuccinimidyl dibutyric urea (DSBU, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1mM TCEP. All the crosslinking reactions were performed at RT for 50 min and then quenched with 20 nM NH HCO . The cross-linked samples in triplicate were vacuum-dried and resuspended in 4% SDS in 50 mM Tris/HCl pH 8.0. Reduction and alkylation were performed with 15 mM TCEP and 25 mM chloroacetamide 30 min at 45 ºC, respectively. Samples were then trypsinized (16 hours, 37 °C) at an enzyme-to-substrate ratio of 1:50 following an automated SP3 protocol 31. Digested samples were resuspended in 1% (v/v) formic acid, 0.5% DMSO for LC-MS/MS analysis. Peptides were analysed by LC-MS/MS in an Exploris480 mass spectrometer (Thermo) coupled to a Vanquish Neo LC system. Peptides were loaded into a trap column (PepMap™ Neo, 5 µm C18, 300 µm x 25 mm) and then separated on an Easy-Spary™ PepMap Neo™ analytical column (C18 2 µm 75 µm x 500 mm) maintained at 50 ºC. An 85-minute gradient was used at a flow rate of 400 nL/min, with solvent A consisting of 0.1% formic acid (FA) and solvent B consisting of 100% acetonitrile (ACN) with 0.1% FA. The gradient ramped from 2% to 25% solvent B over 50 minutes, then from 25% b to 45% solvent B over 20 minutes, followed by a 9-minute wash at 98% Buffer B.
The mass spectrometer was operated in a data-dependent mode, with an automatic switch between MS and MS/MS scans using a top 15 method. Intensity threshold ≥ 5 x 103, dynamic exclusion of 20 sec and excluding charges (+1 and ≥ +8). MS spectra were acquired from 400 to 1500 m/z with a resolution of 60,000 FWHM (200 m/z). Ion peptides were isolated using a 0.7 Th window and fragmented using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with a stepped normalized collision energy of 29, 31 and 33. MS/MS spectra resolution was set to 60,000 (200 m/z). The ion target values were 3 x 106 for MS (maximum IT of 25 msec) and 1 x 105 for MS/MS (maximum IT set to auto, according to the transient length). Aliquots of both the cross-linked and pre-cross-linking samples was digest with trypsin in parallel. Two hundred nanograms of the resulting non-cross-linked peptides were analyzed using a 37-minute gradient on a Vanquis Neo, coupled with an Orbitrap Astral. The Orbitrap Astral was operated under a standard Data-Independent Acquisition (DIA) protocol to optimize protein detection and enhance quantification. Subsequently, DIANN analysis was performed on the pre-cross-linking sample, querying a custom-built FASTA database that included the host expression organism (Sf9 and the baculovirus) the CCD6-RET fusion protein construct, and the UniProt sequences of 525 proteins commonly identified as contaminants over the past decade in proteomic analyses of diverse samples. The proteins identified by DIANN were sorted by intensity and examined for potential contamination. For the cross-linked samples, the top 313 most abundant proteins in the non-cross-linked sample, based on the sum of all precursor intensities as calculated by DIANN, were selected. These proteins were then used to construct a customized FASTA database for MeroX searches. This number was deemed sufficient to model decoy hits and control the false discovery rate (FDR), as MeroX uses a built-in target-decoy strategy at the crosslink spectrum match (CSM) level for reliable error estimation. For MeroX analysis of cross-linked samples, raw files acquired from the Orbitrap Exploris 480 were converted to MZML files using the ProteoWizard ms.convert program. The search parameters for MeroX were configured as follows: protease sites R/P and K/P, with a maximum of three missed cleavages, with K blocked as XL-site. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (C) was set as a fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine (M) and phosphorylation of Ser, Thr, and Tyr were treated as a variable modification. DSBU was chosen as the cross-linker, and MeroX's default parameters were used, considering dead-end reactions with H O and NH , since the cross-linking reaction was quenched with excess ammonium bicarbonate. The precursor and fragment ion precision were set to 5 ppm (MS1) and 10 ppm (MS2), respectively. Identification focused on b and y ion types, with a minimum of three fragments per peptide. Charge states of +2 and higher were selected, and deisotoping was enabled. Precursor mass correction was disabled. RISEUP was chosen as the analysis mode, allowing for one missing ion. Neutral losses were enabled, with a maximum of one loss per fragment. For scoring and FDR calculations, a prescore of 10%, an FDR cutoff of 1%, and a score cutoff of 50 were applied. Given the use of a customized database based on comprehensive sample analysis, the MeroX cRAP database was excluded from the searches.
Finally, each fragmentation spectra were manually inspected and validated. Circular views and further processing of crosslinked residues were done using XiVIEW 32. For cross-linked peptide quantification, raw data were imported into Skyline. Label free quantification of identified cross-linked peptides was performed using the extracted ion chromatogram of the isotopic distribution. Only peaks without interference were used for quantification and manually inspected for correct area integration. The sum of the ion areas was collapsed for each cross-linked peptide and normalized using the total ion intensity of each sample. Data shown are from one experiment with triplicate samples with two technical replicate each. Crosslinked samples were tested by SEC to monitor the formation of dimers versus high-molecular weight species.

Negative staining and electron microscopy.
CCDC6-RET (0.7 M) was placed onto freshly glow-discharged (GloQube, Quorum Technologies) home-made carbon-coated 400 mesh copper electron microscopy (EM) grids. The conditions for glow discharge were: 15 mA, 45“, 0.1 bar. The samples were then incubated for 5 sec at RT. The grids were consecutively placed on top of three distinct 50 μL drops of MilliQ water, striped gently with filter paper for 2 sec and laid on the top of two different 50 μL drops of 1% uranyl acetate and stained for 1 min. Finally, they were stripped gently for 5 sec and air dried. Prepared grids were visualized on a Tecnai G2 Spirit transmission EM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with Lanthanum hexaboride cathode operated at 120 keV. Images were recorded at 61 320 x nominal magnifications on a 4k x 4k TemCam-F416 CPMOS camera (TVIPS), with pixel size of 2.5 Å/pix. For data collection, the open-source software SerialEM (bio3d.colorado.edu/SerialEM) was used under a Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) license. For data processing, open sources software cryoSPARC 33 and Relion were used 34.

Small angle X-ray scattering.
SAXS experiments were conducted at the beamline B21 of the Diamond Light Source (Didcot, UK)35. CCDC6-RET∆CT (40 L, 5 mg/mL) was injected at room temperature into a Superdex 200 Increase 3.2 column connected to an in-line Agilent 1200 HPLC system. The buffer used for the SEC column was the same protein buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1mM DTT). The eluted samples were exposed for 300 s in 10 s acquisition blocks using an X-ray wavelength of 1 Å, and a sample to detector (Eiger 4M) distance of 3.7 m. The data covered a momentum transfer range of 0.0032 < q < 0.34 Å-1. The frames recorded immediately before elution of the sample were subtracted from the protein scattering profiles. The Scåtter software package (www.bioisis.net) was used to analyze data, buffer-subtraction, scaling, merging and checking possible radiation damage of the samples. The R value was calculated with the Guinier approximation assuming that at very small angles q < 1.3/R . The particle distance distribution, D , was calculated from the scattering pattern with GNOM and shape estimation was carried out with DAMMIF/DAMMIN, both programs included in the ATSAS package 36. The proteins molecular mass was estimated with GNOM. Interactively generated PDB-based homology models were made using the program COOT by manually adjusting them into the envelope given by SAXS that could match the experimental scattering data. This was computed with the program FoXS 37.

Structural modelling and molecular dynamic simulations.
Publicly available X-ray crystal structures of different RET kinase constructs, as well as those of related tyrosine kinase domains from catalytic receptors such as EGFR, FGFR (1-3), and the human insulin receptor, were suitably aligned using the Dali server. The RCD+ server 38 was employed to fill in existing gaps in the structurally disordered regions due to lack of electron density. The ATP molecule and the two coordinating, partially hydrated, magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) were carefully placed in an arrangement compatible with transfer of the -phosphate to a peptide substrate (near-attack conformation), as found in the prototypical cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase A (PDB ids. IL3R and 4HPU). This experimental information was complemented with models generated by AlphaFold 3 39 for wild-type RET and the oncogenic CCDC6-RET homodimer, both in the absence and presence of adenosine nucleotides, Mg²⁺, and peptide substrates (accession codes: ma-pcoh8 and ma-b7la0). Additional models of CCDC6-RET in the unstimulated form were obtained with AlphaFold (AF id: J7M8C2, for the single chain in the manual model) and AlphaFold multimer Colab (RETPTC1DIMER_a902d_unrelaxed_rank_001_alphafold2_multimer_v3_model_2_seed_000), in the case of the homodimer. The SWISS-MODEL homology modeling server 40 was also used for validation. Energy minimization and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at 300 K of the systems studied were run in explicit physiological saline solution under periodic boundary conditions using the ff14SB AMBER force field 41 with updated parameters for phosphates 42, TIP3P water molecules and the pmemd.cuda_SPFP engine, as implemented in AMBER 18 running on Nvidia GTX 1080 RTX2080Ti GPUs, essentially as described 43. The cutoff distance for calculating the non-bonded interactions was 9 Å and the smooth particle mesh Ewald method with a grid spacing of 1 Å was used to account for electrostatic interactions. Application of the SHAKE algorithm to all bonds involving hydrogens allowed an integration step of 2.0 fs to be used. Each solvated system was simulated in the absence of any restraints for at least 300 ns during which system coordinates were collected every 0.5 ns for further analysis.
Complementarily, for the respective Michaelis complexes, a time-dependent biasing harmonic potential of 5 kcal mol−1 Å−2 was included -as an extra term in the form of a flat well with parabolic sides- to impose pulsating distance restraints within a range compatible with nucleophilic attack (3.9-4.0 Å) and hydrogen bond formation (2.9-3.1 Å). The molecular graphics program PyMOL v. 2.6 was employed for molecular visualization and figure preparation.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors describe a biochemical and structural study of the CCDC6-RET fusion oncoprotein, which is a highly active kinase consisting of the kinase domain of the RET tyrosie kinase fused to a coiled-coil domain from CCDC6. This extensive work incorporates diverse experimental approaches including enzyme kinetics, mass spectrometry, negative stain EM and SAXS to probe the sturcture and activity of this fusion oncoprotein. While there are some solid novel findings here - the comparison of activity of the intact fusion and isolated kinase domain, time-course mapping of autophosphorylation sites - other findings are not sufficiently fleshed out or conclusively supported by the data presented. In particular, there is a worry that ADP-dependent phosphorylation - one of the more interesting findings presented here - is an artifact of contamination with ATP. The negative stain EM reconstructions and computational modeling of the structure, including with Alphafold models, are fine as far as they go, but I am not convinced that there are important dimer contacts apart from the coiled-coil -- are there contacts between the two kinase domains in the dimer that are important for activity? Contacts between the kinase and coiled-coil from the fusion partner? Additionally distinct structural states for unphosphorylated and phosphorylated dimers are presented based on differences in crosslinking mass spec results, but there is a worry that some of these crosslinks could arise from higher order oligomers rather than intra-dimer interactions. In any case, there is no structure-function work ppresented to test these questions.
Specific comments/concerns:
1. This is clearly a highly active kinase fusion – why is it not already autophosphorylated as purified from insect cells?
Please include the reaction progress curves from the coupled enzyme assay for Fig. 1h and 3b as supplemental figures.
Would be informative with respect to whether there is a lag phase resulting from a requirement of autophosphorylation for full
activity.
2. p.16 Binding tightness – not specific, better to just say “Binding…was evaluated).
3. Fig. 1f. Does not make sense to label x-axis with delta Ti, instead indicate which inhibitor and concentration for each bar.
(and legend incorrectly refers back to itself).
4. With the mass spec autophosphorylation time course experiments, it would be informative to analyze the corresponding
non-phosphorylated species in an analogous manner. The fractional decrease in the non-phoshospho peptides would give
a sense of the stoichiometry of phosphorylation of these many sites…are they major sites with high site-occupancy? Or
detectable but present on a very low proportion of molecules?
5. Why is apparent Km[atp] so different in Fig 1h vs. Fig 3b for the intact fusion proteins? Please provide the Km values for
fig. 3b.
6. There is a very real worry that the apparent ADP-dependent phosphorylation is just an artifact of contamination of the ADP
with ATP. Or that contaminating ATP was carried along with the kinase in the course of enzyme purification. Not clear that
the authors have done anything to address this possibility. A few suggestions: 1) measure ATP content of ADP preparation
using a luciferase assay. Or better yet measure directly by LC/MS. 2) Test activity with beta-32P-labelled ADP. 3) Test
phosphorylation of a peptide substrate in a quantitative way, with peptide in excess. If you start with say 500 nmoles of ADP,
can you phosphorylate most or all of 500 nmoles of peptide? Or do all of the above!
7. In figure 4, what are the Km values for full length and truncation? (they look quite similar). How do we know that the
apparent difference in Vmax in not just a difference in enzyme concentration? Legend not reassuring in this respect – reports
0.2-0.3 uM. Need demonstrated careful measurement of enzyme concentration. At a minimum Coommassie stained gel with
equivalent amounts used, or better to titrate both with a potent Ret kinase inhibitor – show that x micromoles of inhibitor
completely kills x micromoles of enzyme. Also, would be worth looking at the effect on Km[peptide].
8. Figure 5 and associated text was very difficult to follow and full of logical leaps. The lack of side-by-side comparable
experiments with the A-loop mutants in FL vs deltaCT makes it impossible for me to draw any meaningful conclusions.
9. Crosslinking-MS data are interpreted as being intra-dimer, inter-molecular crosslinks. But seems no steps were taken to
ensure that none are inter-dimer crosslinks? (For example SEC after crosslinking to remove any higher order crosslinked
species?)
10. Actually the SDS-PAGE gel with crosslinked protein shows the major species is a smear around 200kDa (presumably
dimer of dimers?), and there is also a pronounced band above 250 kDa. So not reasonable to interpret crosslinks as intra-
dimer.
11. It is clear that phosphorylation changes the pattern of crosslinking, but not clear how the authors arrived at their structural
models. And in any case, given concerns in 9 and 10 above, I feel the structural models are a gross over-interpretation of the
data.
12. What is meant by cis-autophosphorylation? The data suggest autophosphorylation in trans in the context of the dimer –
no clear concentration dependence of autophosphorylation of the dimer, but there is concentration dependence of a
monomeric kinase construct. Is this what the authors mean by “cis” autophosphorylation? I think most would say “the
protomers of the dimer autophosphorylate in trans”. Cis auto-phosphorylation implies that a given kinase domain/subunit
autophosphorylates itself. There is no data that I see here that would test this mechanism (for example preparation of a
defined heterodimer with one active and one inactive subunit and a test of whether the active subunit could phosphorylated
the inactive partner.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The paper by Plaza-Menacho et al aims at describing the enzymatic activity as well as the molecular structure of CCDC6-
RET chimeric oncoprotein. The paper is potentially interesting, with data suggesting that: i) CCDC6-RET is a dual
ATP/ADP-dependent kinase; ii) the activation loop and the c-terminal tail of RET interact modulating protein folding and
activity; iii) CCDC6-RET autophosphorylation occurs in cis. In addition, they also provide an in silico as well as Cryo-EM
and crystallographic analysis to generate a structural model of CCDC6-RET homodimer both in the active as well as
inactive conformation. A major weakness of the paper is that it is not clear which is its principal message since all those
topics tackled in the manuscript are extremely important, but none is demonstrated in a complete and convincing manner.
For example, the ability by CCDC6-RET to use ADP to phosphorylate itself and substrates is striking news. ADP is
classically and paradigmatically unable to provide the beta-phosphate to kinases for phosphorylation. A deeper and more
detailed description of this activity, putting it in comparison with wt RET (not just the TK domain which is a poorly active
kinase) and possibly other chimeric RET fusions, or providing the rate of AMP production (both when supplying ATP or
when using ADP), as well negative controls using other kinases or a kinase dead mutant.
Another example of lack of completeness regards the interaction between the C-tail and the activation loop. Is this true also
for the other forms of RET, and in particular the longer one RET-51 (they have used the RET-9 isoform in the paper)? Is this
influenced by proteins that bind to the c-tail in cells (SHC, ENIGMA, FRS2, IRS1/2, ect)? Again, is this peculiar to CCDC6-
RET or is important also for other RET rearrangements and wt RET?
My suggestion is to study individually each of these aspects, providing a more comprehensive and analytical research study
for each of this topic (maybe using the unpublished data reported in the discussion). I guess that in this way authors would
make a definitive and convincing point on each of the finding they have presented in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The paper of Martín-Hurtado et al. uncovers some of the mechanism and molecular function of the CCDC6-RET fusion
kinase, with important findings on the specificity and autophosphorylation activation. Where the paper is strongest is
biochemical characterization, and especially the phosphorylation assays, which clearly demonstrate the dual specificity of
this kinase. However, it is severely lacking in structural characterization, not because of lack of experiments (which are
plentiful) but because the model derived is not sufficiently supported by data and does not explain the authors’ observation.
Some of the experiments in particular are filtered in ways that inevitably support the proposed model, rather than building a
model from the available data.
It is not the lack of resolution per se (if high resolution could not be attained, that is the way it is), but the lack of a proper
integrative approach that accounts for the experiments carried out. Thus the model derived does not clarify or explain the
observations made in biochemical experiments, and does not come with quantifiable precision/uncertainty. Furthermore, the
methods section is lacking some critical details that would help understand some of the experiments and modeling steps, as
detailed below.
Overall, this leads to a major shortcoming in terms of establishing a structure-function relationship and a mechanistic
understanding of what underpins the kinase activity and regulation. In short, the paper has some major findings on the
specificity and mechanism of the kinase, but then the model presented does not explain how CCDC6-RET achieves its
properties. In particular, little data is presented as to the activation mechanism (it is speculated upon) and as to why this
kinase would have tyrosine and serine specificity or why it would work on both ATP or ADP given the model.
The biochemical and structural data taken by itself is of excellent quality, except for the proteomics and crosslinking MS,
where the experimental analysis and design leaves something to be desidred (see below). The level of support for the
conclusions- i.e. the generation of the structural model and the interpretation of the connection between biochemistry and
structure- is currently weak. If properly characterized however, this paper would provide highly significant findings.
I would recommend accepting the paper only after major revisions.
Major concerns:
- Phosphoproteomics. It seems that there are 2 full replicates, each of which was injected in technical duplicates, but a
single plot is “representative of 2 independent experiments”, rather than showing all 4 traces. As we are being asked to
judge dynamics, the reproducibility of the quantification is quite critical, so at least 3 or 4 full replicas are required, even in
single injection, so that proper quantification and error estimation may be carried out. The variance of a double injection is
low, as expected, but the authors are claiming this is "representative” without even showing all 4 traces. The
phosphoproteomics plot should come with error bars coming from quantification of replicates.
- In the methods section, state the number of full and technical replicates for both crosslinking MS and proteomics.
- Quantitative crosslinking MS: quantitation is not performed across replicates, which are needed when comparing between
conditions. I would expect volcano plots where we can see what residue pairs are significantly changing between apo and
phosphorylated conditions. See for example Tomko et al. Cell 2015 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26451487/). The fact
that a crosslink is detected only in a particular condition, when variance is not estimated, is not indicative of a unique
conformation, especially in DDA.
- Show all detected residue pairs on the structure and provide a distance histogram, as well as coloring the circle plot by
distance. I find it hard to believe that almost all crosslinks detected arise from peptides containing the critical tyrosine, and
there is almost no coverage of the rest of the protein. Does the crosslinking MS support this model? Only an unbiased
mapping of all detected residue pairs at 5% FDR (provided the database did at least include contaminants) can show- one
cannot claim validation after filtering to only have distances within range.
- The structural modeling is perhaps the weakest part of the paper. In fact, there is no methods section for the modeling part,
which comprises a major part of the paper. The results are interspersed with the steps done to assemble the model. The
authors manually generated and adjusted a model by patching a coiled coil alignment and the kinase region. This is then
placed in the negative stain density and presented as a good fit, which is not quantified. Similar thing for the SAXS, where
the authors delete the disordered regions to rejigger them inside the DAMMIN density, only to then say the resulting model is
a good fit with CRYSOL. Are the disordered regions compact or extended? This is exactly the sort of information SAXS may
provide if it is treated as the ensemble solution experiment that it is. The crosslinking MS experiment is similarly presented
as validating the model, but only after filtering crosslinks to within distance and not plotting the full crosslinking MS dataset
on the structure. As a matter of fact, what is the advantage of using the hand made model over the AlphaFold one (or
adjusting the alphafold one)? At least AlphaFold has a confidence metric that shows that it is not confident in the coiled coil
regions. I would encourage the authors to use HADDOCK or the integrative modeling platform (IMP) to integrate SAXS,
negative stain, crosslinking MS and basic structure predictions to generate an ensemble of predicitons based on the data.
Or, the crosslinking MS data can perhaps be used to improve the modeling with AlphaLink2. In both cases, this would then
lead to a model that can be interpreted as it comes with a precision that encodes for the uncertainty
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25173450/) of low resolution and sparse restraints.
- Figure 5 c, “Enzymatic assay performed with CCDC6-RET  CT, WT and activation loop mutants Y900F, Y905 and
Y900/905F (1 M) incubated with increasing concentrations of ATP at a fixed concentration (1.35 mM) of a c-Abl derived
peptide (EAIYAAPFAKKK), I would expect to have five curves but only four are shown. Also the activation loop mutants
used in the essay are presumably from the main text from the protein version lacking the C-terminal domain; please annotate
it in the legend accordingly to WB figures.
- Where are all the phosphosites detected on the structure? Does the model explain how some phosphosites are
phosphorylated before others? Are they near the active site? The pocket is not highlighted in any of the figures. What are the
motifs around the phosphosites? Showing the phosphosites, discussing their position and coloring them by time of
phosphorylation would help address many of these questions. The distinction between cis and trans autophosphorylation
should have a correspondence in the model.
Minor concerns:
- How do the authors explain the upper and lower bands of the western blot in the phosphorylation assays?
- Figure 4f, please show the residue number in the circos plot for better clarity.
- Figures 4 b and d, although clear from figures c and e, state the WT and ΔCT in the legends of the enzymatic assays with
A-loop and abl peptide.
- DSBU is a homobifunctional (not heterobifunctional) crosslinker. It has 2 NHS-ester moieties.
- “In particular, we found that in autophosphorylation and enzyme kinetics experiments, where we evaluated the KM for ATP
in the presence of an excess of peptide susbtrate, a Y905F and double Y900/905F mutants have a loss of function effect,
contrary to the Y900F, that was catalytic competent. “ Please state Figure 5c for better clarity of the reader.
- Figure 8b, kcat/km ratio instead of only kcat should be indicated on the y axis of the bar plot. Please indicate legend with
the different CCDC6-RET concentrations used in the enzymatic activity assay plot in figure 8b.
- Why not AlphaFold3 but filtered by prediction confidence? What does the AlphaFold3 model look like?
- In one of the panels showing the model, highlight the ATP binding site and substrate binding pocket, if possible. Does the
model give hints as to why it would phosphorylate serine and tyrosine? Is the pocket similar to other dual specificity
kinases?
- Show SEC-MALS data, size exclusion traces if possible. The results of the coiled-coil predictor, which in general may be
less accurate than AlphaFodl, can be shown in fewer panels.
- “This residue when mutated appears to have a profound effect on the catalytic activity of the RET fusion product towards a
substrate despite lacking any effect on autophosphorylation (unpublished data).” This is a particularly important point. I
suppose the difference between “data not shown” and “unpublished data” is that these findings lie in another paper that is
also in review? Can there be at least pointing to a preprint?
Technical points:
Crosslinking MS analysis:
- For MeroX analysis, please state clearly how you performed the analysis. E.g., Was precursor correction enabled? For mgf
file (only MS2 data), the software would do this without knowing the real MS1 data, so either turn off that option or inspect the
MS1-precursor level of the cross-links. If you export mzML with also MS1 information, then it would be looking at MS1 data to
perform precursor quadrupolar isolation window correction. For QExactive series of instrument this correction is quite useful,
never tested on Exploris 480. Was RISE-UP mode used? How many proteins were used in the fasta? Fusion protein alone
or with contaminants (cRAP database option in the last panel)? Searching with target-decoy FDR against a single protein
inevitably leads to poor error estimation, as the decoy database is not large enough to model the noise of random
matching.
AlphaFold:
- The authors do not state which version of AlphaFold multimer was used or any of the settings with regards to template and
MSA. It seems the authors may have used colabFold, with relaxation off, given the severe clashes present in the model.
Similar steric clashes are also present in the model the authors built, which shows that the coiled coil prediction server may
have packed the helices a bit too close together, or at the wrong angle.
Data availability:
- We were not given access to the proteomics or crosslinking MS data as the authors did not include the reviewer password
associated with the deposition.
- Is the Skyline file containing the phospho-peptide quantification deposited somewhere?
- Models generated in the study should be deposited in PDB-Dev (integrative models) or ModelArchive (AlphaFold models)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_6:
This is a complex but very interesting and potentially very important manuscript that describes the cis and trans
autophosphorylations that take place in a fusion protein where the N-terminus of CCDC6 is fused to the kinase domain of
RET. This fusion creates a constitutively active dimer that now functions as a driver of tumors in the thyroid. Several RET
fusions have been reported in the past and these gene rearrangements were found in Chernoble following the nuclear
contamination because some of the primary events were found in the thymus where iodine accumulates. While other fusions
with other tyrosine kinases have been reported, including BCR-Abl, which was the first protein shown to cause cancer, this
study with CCDC6-RET is important because it delves more deeply into the properties of this fusion protein. In all cases, the
fusion proteins are thought to be active because the fusion creates a constitutive dimer which is essential for activation of
any of these tyrosine kinases. Usually a transcient dimer forms as a part of the activation process. This paper first shows
convincingly not only that this dimer is constitutively active but also that it phosphorylates many sites that are not typically
reported to be phosphorylation sites in RET. This includes many novel pTyr sites as well as pSer sites and it also includes
site in CCDC6 as well as in RET where CCDC6 is not a normal target for RET. They also show a time frame for these
phosphorylation events which relies on Mass Spectrometry and is very difficult to capture. With mutagenesis they decipher
which of the sites are likely to be biologically important. The authors also suggest that this kinase may be able to use ADP
as a phosphoryl donor. Finally with preliminary negative staining and preliminary and preliminary CryoEM they are able to
build a credible model for this fusion protein. Overall, there are some very important things that we can learn from this
manuscript even though some of the things are likely to be artifactual. Some of the concerns are serious and would likely
require some additional experiment; however, if the authors could satisfactorily address these concerns, then the manuscript
should be re-considered for publication.
Specific Concerns:
1. The mapping of the phosphorylation sites is very detailed and comprehensive and shows very clearly that this fusion
protein is hyperactive and is phosphorylating a lot of spurious sites that are not seen with the native RET. It shows global
dysregulation and also defines lack of specificity. It is important to unambiguously show that this lack of specificity is a
feature of this constitutive dimer. This point should be emphasized.
2. These phosphorylation sites are mostly cis as would be expected. While the authors made this point earlier with Src, this
is an important point and will likely be a conserved feature of all of these oncogenic fusion proteins. The biological
significance of these sites in cells where phosphatases are often constitutively expressed and localized at the same site is
debatable. In contrast to the cis phosphorylations, which can be quite random and meditated whenever a surface hydroxyl
group comes in close proximity to the ATP, the transphosphorylation sites are required for phosphorylation of heterologous
protein substrates so these are likely to be the more physiologically relevant sites. This point should be very clearly made.
3. The trans phosphorylations require correct organization of the Activation Loop and the authors do show how Y900 and
Y905 are more important for activity than the other sites. How these contribute to organization of the Activation Loop is still
unclear and also unclear is the chronology. Is modification of Y900 a required precursor step for the phosphorylation of
Y905? Does their data indicate this stepwise process? If so, it should be articulated very clearly.
4. Importance of targeting. The many random cis auto-phosphorylations suggest that the first cis auto-phosphorylations take
place quickly when then the kinase is first activated. Is this a correct assessment of the data? It makes sense that the
phosphates of ATP, which is initially targeted with low affinity binding by hydrophobic residues that interact with the adenine
ring of ATP, are highly flexible and easily able to phosphorylate any hydroxyl group that comes in close proximity. . In the wt
kinases the phosphorylation sites are very focused and are organized so that only a specific protein is modified, usually on
a single site. This is because the kinase is recruited to a specific site which contains may contain other proteins such as
phosphatases and the downstream proteins that will bind to the pTyr. In this case the kinase will only be transiently
dimerized. This specificity is lost in the fusion protein where the kinase is constitutively activated because it is a dimer but
close to the fusion protein rather that its physiological partner. How does this kinase find its right target?
5. Another point that the authors make is that ADP, as well as ATP, can serve as the donor for phosphorylation. To make this
claim I think it is important that the authors show direct transfer of the beta phosphate using 32P-labeled ATP. An old set of
papers by Ora Rosen, indicated that ATP could be generated directly from a phosphorylated residue at the active site of one
of the PKA regulatory subunits. While such an observation to my knowledge has not been pursued for other kinases, it is still
possible that the phosphates from ATP could somehow be “scrambled”. While ADP may stabilize one of the protomers,
to claim that the phosphate is also transferred from ADP requires the radio-labelled ATP.
6. Heterodimers. Do the authors know if heterodimers are formed between the fusion protein and wt CCDC6?
7. Where is the fusion protein localized in cells? Presumably targeting is mediated improperly by the coiled:coil domains of
CCDC6.
8. Is the CCDC6 homodimer also expressed in cells? Presumably there is one good copy of both RET and CCDC6. Is this
homodimer more stable so that neither free RET nor the CCDC6 dimer are present in these cells that express the fusion
protein? If this is so, then this mutation not only creates an oncogene but also abolishes the normal function of both proteins.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have made important improvements in the revised manuscript. In particular the new data with radiolabeled ATP
and ADP makes a convincing case for the ability of the fusion protein to transfer the b-phosphate of ADP in an
autophosphorylation reaction (although the Figure providewd for review is not helpful in that all traces are identified as ATP
in the legend). However, a number of issues remain.
1. It is unclear that there is any physiological relevance to the transfer of ADP. Experiments performed here are at
concentrations that are ~100 times greater than cellular concentrations, and given the more efficient phosphorylation with
ATP, unclear that there could ever be a cellular condition in which limiting ATP led to phosphorylation with ADP. As the
authors acknowledge, ATP concentrations are ~1000 times that of ADP. The authors suggest that this might differ in certain
subcellular environments, but wildly speculative to suggest that it could differ enough to make this relevant to the activity of
this RET fusion. That said, utilization of ADP by a kinase is an interesting biochemical result.
2. Along the same lines, seems wrong to suggest that high concentrations of ADP "regulate" the RET fusion, when the
concentrations required are ~100x that found in cells (cells would not survive such a concentration of ADP).
3. the authors us of "apo" to refer to the unphosphorylated kinase is confusing. "Apo" typically means without a binding
partner or co-factor. Clearer to refer the the unphosphorylated state as the "unphosphorylated state" or perhaps inactive
state.
4. Authors at least imply that utilization of ADP for autophosphorylation is unique to the RET fusion. But not clear that is does
not also happen with the isolated kinase domain (which has lower catalytic activity overall) but is at a level that is difficult to
detect.
5. The authors appear to have misunderstood or at least incompletely understood my concern about their conclusions
regarding cis vs trans autophosphorylation. I think the authors and I would both agree that their data argue against inter-
dimer phosphorylation as the dominant mechanism. The question is how intra-dimer phosphorylation occurs, which could
either be in cis (each subunit of the dimer phosphorylating itself) or in trans (one submit phosphorylating the other). In the
kinase field, cis-autophosphorylation would ordinarily be taken to mean a given kinase domain phosphorylating itself,
irrespective of its oligomeric state. For example in an RTK dimer, cis autophosphorylation would imply that each subunit in a
dimer transferred a phosphate to its own activation loop, while trans autophosphorylation would mean each transferred a
phosphate to the activation loop of the partner subunit in the dimer. I still do not know for certain what the authors are
concluding here, but as best I can tell there are two possibilities: 1) they are using cis-autophosphorylation to mean that
CCDC6-RET dimers are autophosphorylating themselves, without regard to whether this intra-dimer phosphorylation is
ocuring in cis or in trans. This is a correct interpretation of their data, but a mis-use (or at least a misleading use) of "cis", for
the reasons outlined above. 2) the authors are claiming that intra-dimer phosphorylation occurs in cis - that is, that each
subunit in the dimer transfers a phosphate to itself. I think this is what the interested reader would likely take as the authors
meaning, but as best I can tell, there is not a single experiment presented to discriminate between cis and trans
phosphorylation within a CCDC6-RET dimer. The "gold standard" experiment the authors now present supports intra-dimer
phosphorylation, but does not address whether intradimer phosphorylation is occurring in cis or trans. The authors could
clear all this up by simply avoiding the "cis" designation, and concluding that autophosphorylation occurs in an intra-dimer
manner, but acknowledging that they have not addressed whether this occurs in cis vs trans.
6. to my understanding, phosphotransfer with ATPgammaS (or more precisely, transfer of thiophosphate) typically involves
transfer of the gamma thiophosphate and not transfer of the beta or beta-gamma phosphate unit as the authors suggest here.
I think this experiment detracts, rather than adds to the story.
7.How do the authors reconcile the high-molecular weight species seen in prior SDS-PAGE gel with crosslinked samples
with the clean, dimeric peak seen in the SEC experiment provided in the revision? Presumably this was carried out on a
parallel sample, and not the actual sample used for crosslinking mass spec studies? Was the SDS-PAGE gel of the actual
sample?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors present a much improved version of the manuscript that broadly addresses our concerns, specifically on the
phosphoproteomics and the crosslinking MS quantitation aspects.
There are still 2 areas that present major issues:
- we requested to have all crosslinks of the datasets mapped on the structure. The authors reply to this by saying that only
few crosslinks arise from the site of interest. The issue is that in order to interpret those proposed crosslinks in a structural
context, one would need to understand if the proposed model is validated/consistent with the crosslinking dataset as a
whole. What is the percentage of crosslinks within distance? is the sample overcrosslinked (as another reviewer was
wondering)? Normally this is addressed also with a distogram over the whole dataset. Without this, we have no way of
assessing what is the relevance and reliability of the specific crosslinks highlighted by the authors
- Again, alphafold models are presented without PAE plots or coloring by pLDDT. This is discouraged also by DeepMind
themselves. Indeed, looking at the ModelArchive deposition, one can see that the confidence of the inter-dimer arrangement
of the catalytic lobes is low, as well as the pLDDT scores around the active site and in the ADP itself. A model with ATP can
also be predicted and the difference in pocket conformation (again, with judgment gauged by inspection of pLDDT) can
support or refute some of the arguments being made. Similarly, the fact that this "fits well" with the negative stain data is
presented with no cross-correlation or %ge inside metrics.
In general, while the manuscript has greatly improved in transparency and in overall readability, our objections were that the
model uncertainty is not quantified, the model precision is not quantified, the fit to the data (save for SAXS chi squared) is not
really quantified. These remain problematic. Ultimately, this structure does not have the resolution or interpretability to
explain why this kinase should use ADP as substrate, for example with mutation of R912 that supposedly plays a key role in
the proposed mechanism.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_6:
The authors did an extensive amount of work to address the various specific concerns that were raised by the reviewers. My
major concern was with regard to phosphorylation by ADP. The authors did the critical experiment of using radio-labeled
ADP to show that the bets-phosphate was transferred to the protein. While this may not be physiological, the data

reviewer_comments.reviewer_7:
Dear Authors,
Thank you for submitting the revised manuscript and for addressing some of the previous comments. While the study has
been improved, several important concerns remain that should be clarified to strengthen the significance and rigor of your
work.
1. In your response, you indicate that other RET fusion proteins (e.g., PTC2 and RIα-RET) were used to support the claim
that ADP-dependent phosphorylation is a distinctive feature of CCDC6-RET. However, it is important to note that fusion
partners such as RIα-RET are rare in human cancers, especially when compared to more common and clinically relevant
fusions such as NCOA4-RET (PTC3) or KIF5B-RET. The use of such uncommon variants as primary comparators limits the
generalizability and biological relevance of your conclusions. To more convincingly demonstrate the uniqueness of CCDC6-
RET’s biochemical behavior, direct comparative analyses with frequent RET fusions—particularly those with well-
established roles in oncogenesis—are essential. Furthermore, it appears that these critical comparative data are not
included in Figure 4, which diminishes support for this central claim.

The paper of Martín-Hurtado et al. uncovers some of the mechanism and molecular
function of the CCDC6-RET fusion kinase, with important findings on the specificity and
autophosphorylation activation. Where the paper is strongest is biochemical
characterization, and especially the phosphorylation assays, which clearly demonstrate
the dual specificity of this kinase. However, it is severely lacking in structural
characterization, not because of lack of experiments (which are
plentiful) but because
the model derived is not sufficiently supported by data and does not explain the authors’
observation. Some of the experiments in particular are filtered in ways that inevitably
support the proposed model, rather than building a model from the available data.
It is not the lack of resolution per se (if high resolution could not be attained, that is the
way it is), but the lack of a proper integrative approach that accounts for the experiments
carried out. Thus the model derived does not clarify or explain the observations made in
biochemical experiments, and does not come with quantifiable precision/uncertainty.
Furthermore, the methods section is lacking some critical details that would help
understand some of the experiments and modelling steps, as detailed below.
Overall, this leads to a major shortcoming in terms of establishing a structure-function
relationship and a mechanistic understanding of what underpins the kinase activity and
regulation. In short, the paper has some major findings on the specificity and mechanism
of the kinase, but then the model presented does not explain how CCDC6-RET achieves
its properties. In particular, little data is presented as to the activation mechanism (it is
speculated upon) and as to why this kinase would have tyrosine and serine specificity or
why it would work on both ATP or ADP given the model.
The biochemical and structural data taken by itself is of excellent quality, except for the
proteomics and crosslinking MS, where the experimental analysis and design leaves
something to be desidred (see below). The level of support for the conclusions- i.e. the
generation of the structural model and the interpretation of the connection between
biochemistry and structure- is currently weak. If properly characterized however, this
paper would provide highly significant findings.

This is a complex but very interesting and potentially very important manuscript that
describes the cis and trans autophosphorylations that take place in a fusion protein
where the N-terminus of CCDC6 is fused to the kinase domain of RET. This fusion
creates a constitutively active dimer that now functions as a driver of tumors in the
thyroid. Several RET fusions have been reported in the past and these gene
rearrangements were found in Chernoble following the nuclear
contamination because some of the primary events were found in the thymus where iodine accumulates. While other fusions
with other tyrosine kinases have been reported, including BCR-Abl, which was the first protein shown to cause cancer, this
study with CCDC6-RET is important because it delves more deeply into the properties of this fusion protein. In all cases, the
fusion proteins are thought to be active because the fusion creates a constitutive dimer which is essential for activation of
any of these tyrosine kinases. Usually a transcient dimer forms as a part of the activation process. This paper first shows
convincingly not only that this dimer is constitutively active but also that it phosphorylates many sites that are not typically
reported to be phosphorylation sites in RET. This includes many novel pTyr sites as well as pSer sites and it also includes
site in CCDC6 as well as in RET where CCDC6 is not a normal target for RET. They also show a time frame for these
phosphorylation events which relies on Mass Spectrometry and is very difficult to
capture. With mutagenesis they decipher which of the sites are likely to be biologically
important. The authors also suggest that this kinase may be able to use ADP as a
phosphoryl donor. Finally, with preliminary negative staining and preliminary and
preliminary CryoEM they are able to build a credible model for this fusion protein. Overall,
there are some very important things that we can learn from this manuscript even though
some of the things are likely to be artefactual. Some of the concerns are serious and
would likely require some additional experiment; however, if the authors could
satisfactorily address these concerns, then the manuscript should be re-considered for
publication.
Answer: We are grateful for the referee´s comments and positive evaluation. We agree
this is a complex but very interesting and potentially very important manuscript that
describes for the first time the molecular mechanism of CCDC6-RET autoactivation. We
have tried to experimentally address most of the referee’s comments and concerns, in
particular the experiments that proved beta-phosphate transfer from ADP during the
CCDC6-RET autophosphorylation reaction.
Specific Concerns:
1. The mapping of the phosphorylation sites is very detailed and comprehensive and
shows very clearly that this fusion protein is hyperactive and is phosphorylating a lot of
spurious sites that are not seen with the native RET. It shows global dysregulation and
also defines lack of specificity. It is important to unambiguously show that this lack of
specificity is a feature of this constitutive dimer. This point should be emphasized.
Answer1: Lack of specificity is supported by the very fast kinetics of autophosphorylation
(e.g. activation loop) observed and by the proposed cis-driven mechanism which is
contrary to the native (wild-type) kinase, which is characterized by a temporal and
sequential pattern of (intermolecular) autophosphorylation. This is unexpected, as the
simplest and more predictive working hypothesis was that dimerization will favour
intermolecular phosphorylation between catalytic domains. We have emphasized on this
aspect now in the results and discussion sections in the revised version of the
manuscript, where we state that this lack of specificity is a feature of this constitutive
dimer. See page 31 on the revised version of the manuscript.
20
2. These phosphorylation sites are mostly cis as would be expected. While the authors
made this point earlier with Src, this is an important point and will likely be a conserved
feature of all of these oncogenic fusion proteins. The biological significance of these sites
in cells where phosphatases are often constitutively expressed and localized at the same
site is debatable. In contrast to the cis phosphorylation, which can be quite random and
meditated whenever a surface hydroxyl group comes in close proximity to the ATP, the
transphosphorylation sites are required for phosphorylation of heterologous protein
substrates so these are likely to be the more physiologically relevant sites. This point
should be very clearly made.
Answer 2: We agree with the referee that most of the autophosphorylation sites would
be in cis. This comes in line also with the mechanism of autophosphorylation observed
in some bacterial hybrid histidine kinases as we indicated and referred in the text (see
result section page 28 and discussion on page 33. In the active configuration the catalytic
domain of each of the protomers of the homodimer are facing away from the stem of the
coiled-coil dimeric interface and this is compatible with cis-autophosphorylation. In the
case of c-Src we recently published a study where we dissected a cis-to-trans
autophosphorylation switch at the activation loop that preceded the intermolecular
autophosphorylation of its C-terminal segment (Cuesta-Hernández and Contreras et al.
2023). Whether cis-autophosphorylation is a conserved feature of all of these oncogenic
RET fusion proteins is something that will depend on the monodispersion state of the
functional assemblies (mono-di-oligomeric state) and the contacts that define each of
them. For example, in the case of the PTC2 we found a dynamic equilibrium between
monomer and dimer species, and binding to c-AMP favours the dissociation and
monomeric state of the fusion product, altering its capacity to autoactivate (in this case
delays the process). How this translates to the phosphorylation of heterologous protein
substrates is a critical question and we are currently exploring this aspect by using a
cellular system where cell extract from starved cells are used as a source of substrates
for the recombinant protein to be phosphorylated under different nucleotides stimulation
(work in progress, see also Fig. 2 on this rebuttal letter).
3. The trans phosphorylation require correct organization of the Activation Loop and the
authors do show how Y900 and Y905 are more important for activity than the other sites.
How these contribute to organization of the Activation Loop is still unclear and also
unclear is the chronology. Is modification of Y900 a required precursor step for the
phosphorylation of Y905? Does their data indicate this stepwise process? If so, it should
be articulated very clearly.
Answer 3: This is another interesting and important point raised by the reviewer#6.
Based on our data shown on Fig. 2, activation loop Tyr 900 comes already
phosphorylated when we purify the protein. Upon RET autoactivation, levels of Tyr 905
phosphorylation augment, and as a consequence the levels of mono-phosphorylated Tyr
900 peptide decreased proportionally along the time course. See also the supplementary
information about the stoichiometry analyses for CCDC6-RET activation loop phospho-
sites (supplementary Fig. 2). Crucially Tyr 900 appears to be critical for the stability and
folding of the RET fusion product (specifically to the short C-terminal isoform 9, see also
Fig. 3 rebuttal letter), as a Y900F mutant is not viable and does not expressed properly.
Strickinly, this dependency is lost in a construct lacking the C-terminal segment where a
Y900F mutant is viable, expresses properly and functional (see Fig. 5 on main
manuscript). The fact that a Y900F mutant of the long C-terminal splicing isoform RET
51 is also functional and viable support the notion that there are critical contacts between
(phosphorylated) Y900 and the C-terminal segment of the short C-terminal segment of
RET that control the fold and stability of the oncogenic fusion (see Fig. 3 rebuttal letter).
4. Importance of targeting. The many random cis auto-phosphorylations suggest that the
first cis auto-phosphorylations take place quickly when then the kinase is first activated.
Is this a correct assessment of the data? It makes sense that the phosphates of ATP,
21
which is initially targeted with low affinity binding by hydrophobic residues that interact
with the adenine ring of ATP, are highly flexible and easily able to phosphorylate any
hydroxyl group that comes in close proximity. In the wt kinases the phosphorylation sites
are very focused and are organized so that only a specific protein is modified, usually on
a single site. This is because the kinase is recruited to a specific site which contains may
contain other proteins such as phosphatases and the downstream proteins that will bind
to the pTyr. In this case the kinase will only be transiently dimerized. This specificity is
lost in the fusion protein where the kinase is constitutively activated because it is a dimer
but close to the fusion protein rather that its physiological partner. How does this kinase
find its right target?
Answer 4: The assessment of our data is that the kinetics of autophosphorylation of the
CCDC6-RET fusion product are very quick and much faster that the sequential
autophosphorylation observed by the RET kinase and intracellular domains which
undergo intermolecular autophosphorylation (see Plaza-Menacho et al. Mol Cell 2014).
In a physiological context, the referee is correct about its own assessment and
interpretation in the case of native kinases that are tightly controlled by transient
dimerization, this specificity is lost in the case of the fusion protein where the kinase is
constitutively activated because it is a dimer but close to the fusion protein rather that its
physiological partner. We hypothesize that the C-terminal segment will play a critical role
on this aspect of the signalling process by the oncogenic chimera, as the phosphorylation
sites (e.g. Tyr 1015, Ser1034, Tyr 1062) will serve as docking for adaptor proteins having
a SH2-, or PTB-binding domain and others. The phospho-proteomic data from the
cellular extracts comparing the CCDC6-RET c-terminal splicing isoforms (i.e. 9vs 51,
short vs long) come in line with this working hypothesis (Martín-Hurtado et al. II in
preparation). We have to consider that the cellular localization of the fusion protein is
different from that of the native kinase. CCDC6 is a nuclear protein and interacts with
DNA most likely by the leucine-zipper motifs found in the ordered CCDC6 portion of the
chimera (aa 53-101, see also figure 6 main text), so another hypothesis is that nuclear
substrates may be affected by the signalling of this oncogenic fusion product. We have
made this point clear in the discussion of the revised version of the manuscript (see page
36).

knowledge has not been pursued for other kinases, it is still
possible that the phosphates from ATP could somehow be “scrambled”. While ADP may stabilize one of the protomers,
